meta.title: Who really said "People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Will Rogers really wrote it: a syndicated squib datelined 22 Nov 1932, on page one the next day. The popular version drops "in America" and the punchline.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified on the scanned 1932 front page. Will Rogers did write it — but the version you have seen is trimmed. Here is the full line, dated and sourced.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1879–1935 · American humorist, film actor and syndicated newspaper columnist
answer.sourceLine: Rogers wired it as one of his daily squibs for the McNaught Syndicate, datelined Los Angeles, 22 November 1932; it ran on page one of papers dated 23 November 1932 under the standing head “Will Rogers Says.” The popular wording is verbatim on the scanned front page of The Washington Times ↗ — what has gone missing since is the opening words “in America” and the closing punchline, “It used to be vice versa.”

source.excerpt: I thought he was crazy. He was—by two States. Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke. It used to be vice versa.
trail: 22 November 1932 — Rogers wires the day’s squib to the McNaught Syndicate. The Imperial Valley Press ↗ of El Centro, California prints it datelined “Los Angeles, Nov. 22 (Special),” and the Will Rogers Memorial Museum ↗ dates the item 22 November 1932.

23 November 1932 — It runs on page one of The Washington Times ↗ under “WILL ROGERS Says:” with the notice “Copyright, 1932, by McNaught Syndicate”: “Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke. It used to be vice versa.”

1976 and 1980 — Quote Investigator ↗ documents the drift: a 15 April 1976 Boston Globe reprint deletes “in America,” and both that reprint and The Will Rogers Scrapbook (1980), edited by Bryan B. Sterling, read “the politicians” where the 1932 papers read “their politicians.”
2019 — The historian Ron Chernow revives the quip at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner; the enquiry that followed is what sent Quote Investigator ↗ back to the 1932 originals.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned front page of The Washington Times ↗ of 23 November 1932. The lines just before it are Rogers owning up to a bad call of his own: Arthur Brisbane had bet Mrs. Ned McClain, on Rogers’s porch, that the Republicans would not carry eight states, and Rogers thought that was crazy — Hoover carried six. The column ran in the weeks after the 1932 presidential election.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: About Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, film actor and syndicated columnist
author.bio: Born in 1879 as a citizen of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory — now Oklahoma — Will Rogers turned a vaudeville rope act into the most trusted running commentary in America. From 1922 he wrote a weekly column and from 1926 a brief daily telegram, both syndicated to more than five hundred newspapers, filed in the voice of a man who insisted all I know is just what I read in the papers. He was killed with the pilot Wiley Post when their plane went down in Alaska on 15 August 1935.

misattribution.heading: The words got trimmed, not stolen
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is seriously credited with this line — the attribution is solid. What has gone wrong is the text. The version that circulates is a shortened, slightly re-cut Rogers, and it almost never carries a date.

items.why: Rogers wrote “Everything is changing in America.” Quote Investigator ↗ found “in America” already deleted when US newspapers reprinted the item on 15 April 1976.

Both 1932 front pages read “their politicians as a joke.” The 1976 reprint and The Will Rogers Scrapbook (1980) read “the politicians,” per Quote Investigator ↗, and the aggregators inherited that reading — A-Z Quotes ↗ still prints it that way, as does the museum’s own list.
The whole joke is the reversal, and it is the first thing memes cut. It is right there at the end of the paragraph on page one of The Washington Times ↗ of 23 November 1932.

items.who: Quoted with no date at all
items.why: A-Z Quotes ↗ gives no date, citing only a 1988 reprint of the Scrapbook, and the line does not appear among the sourced quotations collected on Wikiquote ↗. That is why a firmly dated 1932 newspaper squib reads to many people like an unverifiable internet saying.

misattribution.truthLine: Rogers really wrote it, and the date is nailed down: a daily squib for the McNaught Syndicate, datelined Los Angeles 22 November 1932 and printed on page one in papers dated 23 November 1932 — “Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke. It used to be vice versa.” (The Washington Times ↗; origin traced by Quote Investigator ↗.)

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Rogers filed this one in the weeks after the 1932 presidential election, and the column around it is all election talk. He preens a little that Walter Lippmann had actually read something he wrote about debts, then owns up to a call he got wrong: Arthur Brisbane had bet Mrs. Ned McClain, on Rogers’s porch, that the Republicans would not carry eight states, Rogers thought he was crazy, and Hoover came in with six — Brisbane right, by two states. Then he lands the line. Read in place, it is not a complaint about comedians at all. It is a complaint about a political class that had run out of credibility in the depths of the Depression.

That is why it keeps coming back. It was quoted at the 2019 White House Correspondents’ Association dinner by a historian rather than a comedian, which is roughly Rogers’s point running in reverse. And the irony was already his own job description: his columns ran in more than five hundred newspapers ↗, and he was, professionally, a rope-twirling comedian.
context.detailsSummary: The same telegram, punctuated differently in different composing rooms
detailsBody: Even on day one the wording was not fixed. The scan of The Washington Times ↗ sets the tail as its own sentence — “as a joke. It used to be vice versa.” The Imperial Valley Press ↗ ran the same telegram the same morning with the tail attached as a clause, which is also how Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the Ohio printing it cites: “as a joke, when-it-used-to-be-vice-versa.” One telegram, three composing rooms, three slightly different sentences.

Rogers was not moonlighting as a pundit. Per the Oklahoma Historical Society ↗, he wrote a weekly column from 1922 and a brief daily “telegram” after 1926, both syndicated nationally to more than five hundred papers. This squib ran on page one of the Washington Times, set beside the day’s wire story on the appointment to the Senate seat left vacant by the late Senator Wesley L. Jones — not tucked away on a features page.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Will Rogers should receive credit for the words he published in November 1932; earliest citation the Piqua Daily Call, 23 Nov 1932, p.1 col.1, 'Will Rogers says' (McNaught Syndicate); notes a 15 April 1976 Boston Globe reprint deleting 'in America' and reading 'the politicians', and The Will Rogers Scrapbook (1980, ed. Bryan B. Sterling, ch. 12, p. 102, Bonanza Books) also reading 'the politicians'; opens by noting Ron Chernow shared the quip at the 2019 White House Correspondents' Association dinner. Post dated April 30, 2019.

Front page of The Washington Times, 23 November 1932, under the head 'WILL ROGERS Says:', contains verbatim: 'Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke. It used to be vice versa.' followed by the notice '(Copyright, 1932, by McNaught Syndicate)'. Confirmed both in the LOC ALTO full text and visually in an IIIF page-image crop. Adjacent page-one story: 'GRAMMER GIVEN SENATE SEAT', on the seat of the late Senator Wesley L. Jones.

Front page of the Imperial Valley Press (El Centro, Calif.), 23 November 1932, carries the same Will Rogers telegram datelined 'LOS ANGELES, Nov. 22. (Special)', including 'Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians serious[ly], and their politicians as a joke, when it used to be vice versa.' plus the preceding Walter Lippmann and lost-election-bet passages. Confirmed via the LOC ALTO full text (this item's IIIF tiles render too low-resolution for a visual check).

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum's quotes page carries: 'Everything is changing in America. People are taking their comedians seriously and the politicians as a joke, when it used to be visa versa. - November 22, 1932', and the site footer reads 'Copyright, Will Rogers Memorial Museum 2025'.

A-Z Quotes prints the quote as 'Everything is changing. People are taking their comedians seriously and the politicians as a joke.' with no date, citing only The Will Rogers Scrapbook (1988), Random House Value Publishing.

Wikipedia gives Will Rogers's dates as 4 November 1879 – 15 August 1935, born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory; syndicated by McNaught Syndicate 1922–1935, weekly column from 1922 and daily 'Will Rogers Says' from 1926; died in a plane crash in Alaska with pilot Wiley Post.

The Oklahoma Historical Society encyclopedia entry states Rogers began a weekly column in 1922 and a brief daily 'telegram' after 1926, and that both were syndicated to more than five hundred newspapers; born 4 November 1879, died 15 August 1935.

Wikiquote's Will Rogers page does NOT contain this quotation — verified by retrieving the raw wikitext and inspecting every occurrence of 'comedian'; none match this line. It is cited on the page only as a general collection of sourced Rogers quotations, and is described honestly as not containing this one.
